newsitem.title: JAPAN: Key man in Japan's Okinawa is US educated scholar.
newsitem.headline: Key man in Japan's Okinawa is US educated scholar.

text.p: The man leading efforts to close huge U.S. bases on Japan's southern Okinawa island, the subject of a referendum on Sunday, is a U.S.-educated scholar who fought in the epic 1945 Battle of Okinawa.
Governor Masahide Ota says the poll, in which Okinawans will vote on whether to "streamline" the bases, is not about anti-Americanism or a device to win more subsidies from the central government.
"More than anything else, this referendum is about citizens' will to have self-rule," soft-spoken Ota told reporters on Thursday. "It is a step towards achieving true democracy."

Last week when Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's party floated plans to increase subsidies for Okinawa, Ota rejected them, saying there could be no economic development without the return of the bases.
Voters are expected to back him strongly in the referendum.
Although standing up to the government, Ota has not joined a handful of Okinawan extremists who demand independence from Tokyo.
Ota, 71, is a renowned author of some 40 books on the bloody 1945 battle, Okinawa's politics and history.
His wartime credentials as a battlefront soldier enable him to tower over many younger Japanese politicians, including Hashimoto, who was only eight years old at the time of Japan's surrender.
Since a rape case involving U.S. soldiers a year ago, Ota has led his prefecture's bitter struggle against the Tokyo government to close U.S. bases.
Ota's message has been simple: Why must crowded Okinawa, 51 years after the battle, still host 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan?
On August 28, Ota lost what many Okinawan politicians saw as a humiliating Supreme Court decision over his campaign to block the forced appropriation of land for U.S. bases.
The expected yes vote on Sunday will be a stronger political weapon for Ota than a Supreme Court decision over legal technicalities.
A substantial majority in favour of the proposition could strengthen his stance against the central government, which in turn might threaten U.S. security commitments in the region.

The U.S. military withdrawal from the Philippines in 1992 has increased the strategic importance of bases on Okinawa, including those for an entire Marine Corps division and the important Kadena air base.
Even before he was elected governor in 1990, Ota had consistently attacked Japan's "double standards" in dealing with Okinawa's U.S. bases.

"Since the 1970s, U.S. military facilities on Japan's main islands have decreased in area by 60 percent. On Okinawa, the figure is 15 percent. Why the discrepancy?" Ota told the prefectural assembly last year.

In 1945 as the war threatened Okinawa, Ota, then a 19-year-old student at the elite Okinawa Teacher's College, was drafted into the army as an auxiliary in the Tekketsu Kinno-tai, the "Serve the Emperor with Blood and Iron" unit.
Ota's duty was to run and distribute news leaflets to units and residents fighting in the front, a hazardous mission.

He witnessed brutal treatment of his fellow islanders at the hands of fanatical Japanese soldiers, who forced many of them to commit suicide or others who summarily executed Okinawans suspected of spying for the U.S. army.
After the war, Okinawa was placed under harsh U.S. military rule until 1972 when most of the land for the 40 odd bases here was first appropriated from landowners.
But during this time, U.S. authorities did provide chances for higher learning for many islanders, including Ota who graduated from Syracuse University Graduate School in New York State.
He later became professor of sociology at Ryukyu Univeristy and has also taught at the East-West Center in Hawaii.
